First Warn Forecast: Monday, August 10, 2026

Dangerous Heat Continues Through Wednesday
Heat Index Values of 100° to 110°
Late-Week Heat Relief Now Less Certain

If you were counting down the days until Thursday's promised break from the heat, I have some unfortunate news: Mother Nature may be changing the agreement.

Dangerous heat and humidity will continue across Missouri and Illinois through at least Wednesday, with Extreme Heat Warnings and Heat Advisories remaining in effect. Temperatures will climb well into the 90s again today and Tuesday, while high humidity pushes afternoon heat index values into the 100 to 110 degree range.

A few showers and thunderstorms moving through western and central Missouri early this morning may make it into portions of the area, primarily along and north of Interstate 70. These storms should weaken as they move east, and severe weather is not expected. Some additional cloud cover could hold temperatures down a few degrees across northeastern Missouri and west-central Illinois, but unfortunately, that doesn't necessarily mean much relief from the heat. Higher humidity in those areas will keep heat index values elevated.

For most of us, today will be another brutally hot August afternoon.

Actual temperatures will climb into the middle and upper 90s, with the highest heat index values developing along the Interstate 70 corridor and into southwestern Illinois. Many communities will experience conditions that feel between 105 and 110 degrees during the hottest part of the afternoon.

Tonight won't provide much relief either. Temperatures will remain warm and humidity will stay high, creating another muggy August night before we do it all over again Tuesday.

Tuesday will feature temperatures once again climbing into the middle and upper 90s. Dew points in the middle 70s will combine with that heat to produce another afternoon of widespread 100 to 110 degree heat index values.

With several consecutive days of dangerous heat, the cumulative effects become increasingly important. Your body needs an opportunity to cool down, and warm, humid nights make that more difficult. If you work outdoors, take frequent breaks in air conditioning or shade, drink plenty of water, and don't wait until you feel thirsty. Check on older neighbors and family members, and make sure pets have access to shade, fresh water, and a cool environment.

What Happened to Thursday's Cooldown?

This is where the forecast has changed.

Over the past several days, forecast guidance suggested a cold front would push through the region Wednesday into Thursday, bringing widespread rain and a significant break from the heat.

Newer guidance isn't nearly as enthusiastic about that idea.

The upper-level ridge responsible for our heat now appears likely to remain stronger across the Mid-Mississippi Valley. That could prevent the cold front from pushing very far south, potentially causing it to stall across northern Missouri and southern Iowa.

If that happens, northeastern Missouri and west-central Illinois may receive at least some relief from the heat, while central and southeastern Missouri and southwestern Illinois remain firmly planted in the hot and humid air.

In other words, Thursday may not provide the widespread relief we were previously expecting.

There is still enough uncertainty that I'm not ready to completely remove the possibility of cooler weather, but confidence has decreased considerably. Temperatures late this week could vary significantly depending on exactly where that front eventually stalls.

Rain Chances Are Changing Too

The position of the front also has major implications for rainfall.

Showers and thunderstorms remain possible Wednesday into Thursday, but the potential for widespread heavy rainfall across our area has decreased compared to previous forecasts. Current guidance suggests much of the heavier rain may remain farther north across southern Iowa and northern Missouri.

Rainfall amounts across much of our region may be relatively light, generally around one-tenth to one-half inch across northern areas, with even lower amounts possible farther south.

That's a significant change from earlier forecasts that suggested multiple rounds of heavy rainfall and a more substantial flash flooding threat across the region.

We'll continue watching this carefully because summertime boundaries have a habit of moving around, and relatively small changes in the position of the front could have a major impact on both rainfall and temperatures.

Looking Toward the Weekend

Unfortunately, there are indications that the upper-level ridge could maintain its grip on the region into the weekend.

If the cold front remains north of us, temperatures across much of Missouri and Illinois could remain above average, and potentially impactful heat may continue or return this weekend. Forecast confidence decreases considerably beyond Wednesday, so it's too early to determine exactly how hot we'll get or whether additional heat headlines will be necessary.

The important message this morning is that we should no longer count on Thursday bringing an end to the heat.

What You Need to Know
Extreme Heat Warnings and Heat Advisories remain in effect as dangerous heat continues.
Afternoon heat index values will reach 100 to 110 degrees today and Tuesday.
Dangerous heat and humidity will likely continue through Wednesday.
A few showers are possible this morning, primarily along and north of Interstate 70.
Rain chances increase Wednesday into Thursday, but expected rainfall amounts have decreased.
The cold front may stall farther north than previously expected, meaning the anticipated late-week cooldown is now much less certain.
Above-average temperatures and potentially dangerous heat could continue or return into the weekend.

Forecasts change as new information arrives, and this is a good example of why we continue watching trends rather than locking onto one model solution several days in advance. Yesterday, widespread relief looked increasingly likely. Today, the atmosphere is telling us that stubborn ridge may have other plans.

For now, continue taking the heat seriously. We'll keep watching that front closely over the next couple of days to determine whether it can finally break through and give us some relief.

First. Accurate. Trusted.

That's your First Warn Forecast.
severeNarrative:
First Warn Forecast & Severe Weather Outlook Update
11:50 AM CDT | Wednesday, June 17, 2026
First Warn Weather Alert Day
Headlines
Severe thunderstorms remain likely this afternoon and evening across Missouri and Illinois.
Damaging winds up to 85 mph, large hail up to 2.5 inches, and several tornadoes remain possible.
The greatest threat locally remains across eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois, including the St. Louis metro area.
Strong southwest winds will gust between 40 and 50 mph outside of thunderstorms.
Peak severe weather threat for the St. Louis area remains between 6 PM and 9 PM.

A potentially dangerous severe weather outbreak remains on track across portions of Missouri and Illinois this afternoon and evening. There has been little change in the overall forecast since this morning. The Storm Prediction Center continues to highlight much of eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois in an Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5) for severe weather, while portions of central Illinois remain under a Moderate Risk (Level 4 of 5) where the highest threat for significant severe weather exists.

An intense cluster of thunderstorms that developed overnight across Iowa produced wind gusts exceeding 90 mph and continues to influence the forecast across Illinois late this morning. The primary outflow boundary currently extends from far northeast Missouri into portions of south-central Illinois. This boundary will likely serve as a focus for severe thunderstorm development later today.

Strong sunshine south of the boundary is allowing temperatures to rapidly climb through the 80s while dew points remain in the upper 60s and lower 70s. Combined with an exceptionally strong wind field aloft, conditions remain favorable for supercells capable of producing all severe weather hazards.

While morning storms may slightly alter where the greatest risk ultimately develops, confidence remains high that numerous severe thunderstorms will develop this afternoon and continue through the evening hours.

Primary Threats

🌪 Several Tornadoes Possible

A few strong tornadoes remain possible.
Greatest tornado threat remains across central Illinois.
Tornadoes remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois, especially near any lingering outflow boundaries.

💨 Destructive Winds Possible

Widespread damaging winds of 60 to 80 mph.
Isolated wind gusts exceeding 85 mph remain possible.
Significant tree damage and widespread power outages could occur.

🧊 Large to Very Large Hail

Large hail remains possible with discrete supercells.
Hailstones up to 2.5 inches in diameter may occur.
Timing Across Missouri and Illinois
1 PM - 3 PM

The first severe thunderstorms are expected to develop across northeast Missouri and portions of west-central Illinois. Areas near Quincy, Kirksville, Palmyra, Hannibal, and surrounding communities should closely monitor conditions.

3 PM - 6 PM

The severe weather threat expands southeast into central Missouri and western Illinois. Columbia, Jefferson City, Mexico, Bowling Green, Troy, and portions of the northern St. Louis metro could see supercells capable of producing tornadoes, very large hail, and destructive winds.

6 PM - 9 PM

This remains the peak severe weather window for the St. Louis metropolitan area and much of eastern Missouri and western Illinois. Storms may become more widespread during this period while maintaining the potential to produce damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes. Residents from St. Louis and St. Charles to Edwardsville, Belleville, Alton, Farmington, and surrounding communities should be prepared to act quickly if warnings are issued.

9 PM - Midnight

Storms are expected to organize into a line extending from central Missouri into southern Indiana. Damaging straight-line winds become the primary threat as storms shift into southeast Missouri and southern Illinois. Heavy rainfall and localized flooding may also develop overnight.

Local First Warn Outlook

The highest confidence for severe weather today exists across the Enhanced Risk area covering much of eastern and central Missouri, including Columbia, Jefferson City, the St. Louis metro, northeast Missouri, and west-central Illinois.

Farther south, a Slight Risk extends across southern Missouri and southern Illinois, including Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon. Severe thunderstorms remain possible in these areas, but storm coverage and intensity may be somewhat lower than locations farther north.

The lowest severe weather threat remains across the Missouri Bootheel and far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border where a Marginal Risk remains in place. However, isolated severe storms cannot be ruled out.

Threat Levels

🔴 Moderate Risk (Level 4 of 5)

Central Illinois
Areas northeast of Springfield, Illinois
Greatest potential for strong tornadoes and destructive winds

🟤 Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5)

Northeast Missouri
Central Missouri
Eastern Missouri
St. Louis Metro
West-central Illinois
Southwest Illinois

🟡 Slight Risk (Level 2 of 5)

Southern Missouri
South-central Missouri
Southeast Missouri
Southern Illinois
Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon

🟢 Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 5)

Missouri Bootheel
Far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border
Areas south of Poplar Bluff and near Paducah
Additional Concern: Strong Winds Outside of Storms

Even outside of thunderstorms, strong southwest winds will continue through the afternoon. Sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph with gusts of 40 to 50 mph are expected. Loose outdoor objects should be secured, and travel may become difficult for high-profile vehicles.

Thursday Outlook

The cold front responsible for today's severe weather will gradually move south of the region overnight. Showers and a few thunderstorms may linger into Thursday, especially across southeast Missouri and southwest Illinois. Cooler temperatures in the 70s and lower 80s will provide a welcome break from today's heat and humidity.

Bottom Line

There has been little change in the forecast thinking since this morning. The atmosphere remains primed for severe thunderstorm development this afternoon and evening. While the greatest threat for strong tornadoes remains across central Illinois, all severe weather hazards remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois.

The St. Louis metro remains in the corridor for severe weather between 6 PM and 9 PM, with damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes all possible. Everyone across the First Warn viewing area should remain weather aware and have multiple ways to receive warnings throughout the day and tonight.

First Warn Weather: First. Accurate. Trusted.
